source: According to the theory of central-place foraging, traveling to a distant destination is an expensive investment in terms of time and energy compared to traveling to a nearby destination (Orians and Pearson, 1979; Bell, 1990).

source: Therefore, animals are expected to prefer reducing the time and distance of travel to the food patch and thus will travel farther only when their prey is not sufficiently available near the central place.

source: We thus hypothesize that, in times of abundant food, birds will optimize energy conservation by foraging closer to the colony (Orians and Pearson, 1979; Olsson et al., 2008).

claim: Higher food density will facilitate a higher rate of visits at the nest.
source: Since breeding swifts may maximize food provisioning to the young, the visitation rate could also be tailored to the abundance of insects (Pyke, 1984; Schoener, 1971; Orians and Pearson, 1979) such that higher food density will facilitate a higher rate of visits at the nest (Pyke, 1984; Kramer and Nowell, 1980) (Prediction 5).

claim: A bird's flight speed when feeding its young is expected to vary with food abundance, with an increase in flight speed with greater food abundance.

evidence: This is a prediction of the study based on theory and supported by citations.

claim: The timing of morning emergence from the colony and evening return to the colony is affected by predation risks and the optimization of foraging time in relation to food abundance.
source: The timing of morning emergence from the colony and evening return to the colony is affected by a number of factors (Bednekoff and Houston, 1994; Bonter et al., 2013; Amichai and Kronfeld-Schor, 2019; Salamolard and Weimerskirch, 1993; Harding et al., 2007; Metcalfe and Ure, 1995). These include predation risks that vary throughout the daily cycle and the optimization of foraging time in relation to food abundance.
evidence: This is a statement about factors affecting timing behavior supported by citations.

claim: Swifts will arrive at the colony earlier for roosting when food abundance is sufficiently high.
source: We specifically predict that swifts will arrive at the colony earlier for roosting when food abundance is sufficiently high to provide enough food for their own and their young's needs (Prediction 7).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: If insect abundance is correlated in time, swifts' departure time will be delayed when the abundance of insects on the previous day is higher.
source: If insect abundance is correlated in time such that birds may be able to predict insect abundance based on that of the previous day, we expect the swifts' departure time to be delayed when the abundance of insects on the previous day is higher (Prediction 8) as there is no need to maximize the foraging duration if food is abundant and this could reduce predation risk by avian predators that are active early in the morning (Lang et al., 2019; Roth and Lima, 2007).
evidence: This is a conditional prediction of the study based on theoretical reasoning and supported by citations.

claim: Swifts' emergence times are expected to correlate with the roosting time from the previous night if insect abundance is temporally correlated.
source: Consequently, the predicted swifts' emergence times are expected to correlate with the roosting time from the previous night (Prediction 9a).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: The movement traffic rate varied substantially between different days during the swifts' breeding season, with a minimum of 164.4 and a maximum of 2518.9 insects km–1 hr–1.
source: The movement traffic rate (MoTR) (1207.7 ± 566.7 insects km–1 hr–1) varied substantially between different days during the swifts' breeding season, with a minimum of 164.4 and a maximum of 2518.9 insects km–1 hr–1 (n = 31 days; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on radar measurements, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: No seasonal trend was found in MoTR.
source: No seasonal trend was found in MoTR (Spearman's rank correlation between the ordinal date and the MoTR, ρ = −0.007, p=0.971, n = 31 days; Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: A significant negative effect of MoTR on the swifts' average distance from the breeding colony was found.
source: We found a significant negative effect of the MoTR on the swifts' average distance from the breeding colony (Prediction 1) (estimate <−0.001, t = −5.27, p<0.001, n = 31 days, Gamma Generalized Linear Model [GLM]; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: A significant negative effect of MoTR was found in relation to the birds' maximum distance from the breeding colony.
source: Similarly, a significant negative effect of MoTR was also found in relation to the birds' maximum distance from the breeding colony (Prediction 2) (estimate = −1.818, t = −3.52, p=0.001, n = 31 days, Gaussian GLM; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: No effect of MoTR on the daily route was found.
source: We found no effect of MoTR on the daily route (Prediction 3) (estimate <−0.001, t = −1.65, p=0.123, n = 15 days, Gamma GLM) and on the duration of foraging (Prediction 4) (estimate = 0.029, t = 1.05, p=0.315, n = 15 days, Gaussian GLM).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical analysis.

claim: No effect of MoTR on the duration of foraging was found.
source: We found no effect of MoTR on the daily route (Prediction 3) (estimate <−0.001, t = −1.65, p=0.123, n = 15 days, Gamma GLM) and on the duration of foraging (Prediction 4) (estimate = 0.029, t = 1.05, p=0.315, n = 15 days, Gaussian GLM).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical analysis.

claim: The frequency of visits at the breeding colony was significantly and positively affected by MoTR.
source: The frequency of visits at the breeding colony (Prediction 5) (see the average model in Table 2) was significantly and positively affected by MoTR (estimate = 0.001, t = 3.78, p<0.001, n = 31 days, Gamma GLM; Figure 1D) and negatively affected by the distance of the birds from the breeding colony (estimate <−0.001, t = 2.03, p=0.043, n = 31 days).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on statistical analysis, with reference to Table 2 and Figure 1D.

claim: The frequency of visits at the breeding colony was negatively affected by the distance of the birds from the breeding colony.

claim: There was no effect of MoTR on the average flight speed.

claim: The time of arrival at the breeding colony for nighttime roosting was significantly and negatively affected by the MoTR.

claim: Birds arrived earlier to roost in days characterized by abundant insect prey.

claim: The duration of nighttime roosting was significantly and positively influenced by the evening arrival time to the colony on the prior day.
